'''Katherine Freese''' (born 8 February 1957<ref name="Physics2016">{{Cite journal|url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/do/10.1063/pt.5.031149/full/|doi=10.1063/pt.5.031149|title=Katherine Freese|journal=Physics Today|year=2016|url-access=subscription}}</ref>) is a [[theoretical astrophysics|theoretical astrophysicist]]. She is currently a professor and Director of the Weinberg Institute for Theoretical Physics at the [[University of Texas at Austin]], where she holds the Jeff and Gail Kodosky Endowed Chair in Physics.<ref>{{cite web |title=The University of Texas Austin Department of Physics |url=https://physics.utexas.edu/directory/katherine-freese |website=Directory |publisher=The University of Texas Austin |access-date=16 March 2026}}</ref> She is known for her work in [[theoretical cosmology]] at the interface of [[particle physics]] and [[astrophysics]].

==Education and academic career==
Freese received her BA from [[Princeton University]], one of the first women to major in physics at Princeton.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.browndailyherald.com/2016/09/20/university-michigan-professor-delves-dark-matter/|title=University of Michigan professor delves into dark matter|last=Renken|first=Elena|date=2016-09-20|work=Brown Daily Herald|access-date=2018-02-03|language=en-US}}</ref> She obtained her MA from [[Columbia University]], and her PhD at the [[University of Chicago]] from advisor [[David Schramm (astrophysicist)|David Schramm]].<ref name="Siegfried2014" /> After postdoctoral fellowships at [[Harvard University]], at the [[Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics]] at [[University of California, Santa Barbara]], and as a Presidential Fellow at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], she became an assistant professor at [[MIT]]. She moved to the [[University of Michigan]] in Ann Arbor, where she was the George E. Uhlenbeck Professor of Physics.<ref name="Siegfried2014" /> Freese has worked as the associate director of the Michigan Center for Theoretical Physics.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/120424-dark-matter-collisions-humans-wimps-physics-space-science|title=Dark Matter Hits the Average Human Once a Minute?|last=Major|first=Jason|website=[[National Geographic Society]]|language=en-gb|date=2012-04-26|access-date=2024-10-27}}</ref> In September 2014, she assumed the position of director of Nordita, the [[Nordic Institute for Theoretical Physics]], in Stockholm, and holds a position as visiting professor of physics at [[Stockholm University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://source.washu.edu/2021/03/physicist-freese-explores-dark-side-of-universe-in-mcdonnell-lecture/|title=Physicist Freese explores dark side of universe in McDonnell lecture|last=Ogliore|first=Talia|website=[[Washington University in St. Louis]]|language=en-gb|date=2021-03-05|access-date=2024-10-27}}</ref> In 2019, Freese moved to the [[University of Texas at Austin]], where she holds the Jeff and Gail Kodosky Endowed Chair in Physics.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cns.utexas.edu/news/katherine-freese-has-ideas-to-support-detection-of-dark-matter|title=Katherine Freese Has Ideas to Support Detection of Dark Matter|website=cns.utexas.edu|language=en-gb|access-date=2019-09-25}}</ref>

==Contributions==
Freese has contributed to early research on [[dark matter]] and [[dark energy]]. She was one of the first to propose ways to discover dark matter.<ref>{{cite journal|first=Andrzej|last=Drukier|author2=Katherine Freese |author3=David Spergel |author3-link=David Spergel |title=Detecting Cold Dark Matter Candidates|journal=[[Physical Review D]]|volume=33|issue=12|pages=3495–3508|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.33.3495 |bibcode = 1986PhRvD..33.3495D |pmid=9956575 |year=1986 }}</ref> Her idea of indirect detection in the Earth is being pursued by the [[IceCube Neutrino Observatory]] experiment,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Freese|first=Katherine|title=Can Scalar Neutrinos or Massive Dirac Neutrinos be the Missing Mass|journal=Physics Letters|volume=B167|issue=3|pages=295–300|doi=10.1016/0370-2693(86)90349-7 |bibcode = 1986PhLB..167..295F|year=1986 }}</ref> and the "wind" of dark matter particles felt as the Earth orbits the [[Milky Way]] (work with [[David Spergel]]) is being searched for in worldwide experiments. Her work decisively ruled out [[MACHO]] (Massive compact halo object) dark matter in favor of [[WIMPs]] (weakly interacting massive particles).<ref>{{cite news |last=Glanz |first=James |title=In the Dark Matter Wars, Wimps Beat Machos |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=February 29, 2000 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/02/29/science/in-the-dark-matter-wars-wimps-beat-machos.html}}</ref> She has proposed a model known as "[[Cardassian]] expansion," in which dark energy is replaced with a modification of [[Einstein's equations]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Overbye |first=Dennis |title=What Is Gravity, Really? |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=November 11, 2003 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/11/11/science/what-is-gravity-really.html}}</ref> Recently she proposed a new theoretical type of star, called a [[Dark star (dark matter)|dark star]], powered by dark matter annihilation rather than fusion.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Freese|first=Katherine |author2=Bodenheimer, Peter |author3=Spolyar, Douglas |author4=Gondolo, Paolo |title=Stellar Structure of Dark Stars: A First Phase of Stellar Evolution Resulting from Dark Matter Annihilation
|journal=[[The Astrophysical Journal]]|volume=685|issue=2|pages=L101–L104| doi=10.1086/592685|arxiv = 0806.0617|bibcode =   2008ApJ...685L.101F |year=2008|s2cid=16088040 }}</ref>

Freese has also worked on the beginnings of the universe, including the search for a successful inflationary theory to kick off the [[Big Bang]]. Her natural inflation model <ref>{{cite journal|first=Katherine|last=Freese|author2=Joshua Frieman |author3=Angela Olinto |title=Natural Inflation with Pseudo-Nambu Goldstone Bosons|journal=[[Physical Review Letters]]|volume=65|pages=3233–3236|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.65.3233 |bibcode = 1990PhRvL..65.3233F |year=1990 |issue=26|pmid=10042817}}</ref> is a theoretically well-motivated variant of inflation; it uses axionic-type particles to provide the required flat potentials to drive the expansion. In 2013, observations made by the [[European Space Agency]]'s [[Planck Satellite]] show that the framework of natural inflation matches the data.<ref>{{cite journal|first=Planck|last=Collaboration|title=Planck 2013 Results XXII: Constraints on Inflation|arxiv=1303.5082 |bibcode = 2014A&A...571A..22P|doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201321569|volume=571|year=2014|journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics|page=A22|s2cid=53621995}}</ref> This is now strongly disfavoured by the more recent Planck 2018 and BICEP2/Keck data.<ref>{{cite journal|first=Planck|last=Collaboration|title=Planck 2018 results. X. Constraints on inflation|arxiv=1807.06211 |bibcode = 2020A&A...641A..10P|doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201833887|volume=641|year=2020|journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics|page=A10}}</ref> She has studied the [[Ultimate fate of the universe]], including the fate of life in the universe.<ref>[[Philip Ball]], [https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg17523545.900-never-say-die.html], "Never Say Die", ''[[New Scientist]]'', Aug. 2002</ref>

Freese has served on the board of the [[Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in Santa Barbara and the board of the [[Aspen Center for Physics]].<ref name="Physics2016" /> From 2008 to 2012 she was a councilor and member of the executive committee of the [[American Physical Society]],<ref name="Physics2016" /> She has also served as a member of the board for the [[Oskar Klein Centre for Cosmoparticle Physics]] in Stockholm.<ref name="Siegfried2014" />

== Honors ==

Freese was elected Fellow of the American Physical Society in 2009. She received a [[Simons Foundation]] Fellowship in Theoretical Physics in 2012.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.simonsfoundation.org/grant/simons-fellows-in-theoretical-physics/?tab=awardees|title=Simons Fellows in Theoretical Physics|access-date=2020-04-29}}</ref> In September 2012, Freese was awarded an honorary doctorate (honoris causa) from the [[Stockholm University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.su.se/english/about/ceremonies/honorary-doctorates-2012-1.96994|title=Honorary doctorates 2012 - Stockholm University|website=www.su.se|access-date=2020-03-03|archive-date=2020-03-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200303183055/https://www.su.se/english/about/ceremonies/honorary-doctorates-2012-1.96994|url-status=dead}}</ref> She was awarded the 2019 Julius Edgar [[Lilienfeld Prize]] from the [[American Physical Society]] "For ground-breaking research at the interface of cosmology and particle physics, and her tireless efforts to communicate the excitement of physics to the general public." In 2021 she was awarded the University of Chicago Alumni Professional Achievement Award. In 2020 she was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2020-nas-election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200428010617/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2020-nas-election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 28, 2020|title=2020 NAS Election|publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]]|date=April 27, 2020|access-date=2020-04-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cns.utexas.edu/news/three-ut-austin-faculty-elected-to-national-academy-of-sciences|title=Three UT Austin Faculty Elected to National Academy of Sciences|date=April 27, 2020|access-date=2020-04-30|archive-date=2021-02-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209014656/https://cns.utexas.edu/news/three-ut-austin-faculty-elected-to-national-academy-of-sciences|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Freese was born in [[Freiburg, Germany]] in 1957.<ref name="Physics2016" /> She is the daughter of Dr. Elisabeth Bautz and [[Ernst Freese]], a molecular biologist.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/04/04/obituaries/ernst-freese-64-dies-a-molecular-biologist.html|title=Ernst Freese, 64, Dies; A Molecular Biologist|date=1990-08-04|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=2024-10-27|language=en-US}}</ref> Her brother, Andrew Freese, deceased, was Chief of Neurosurgery at Brandywine Hospital, and performed the first surgery for gene therapy on humans.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.inquirer.com/obituaries/dr-andrew-freese-neurosurgeon-gene-therapy-obituary-20210706.html|title=Dr. Andrew Freese, noted neurosurgeon and pioneer of gene therapy, dies at 61|date=2021-07-06|last=Russ|first=Valerie|newspaper=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]|access-date=2024-10-27|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Popular science==
Freese has written a review for the general educated public on dark matter and energy as they relate to recent research in cosmology and particle physics, titled ''The Cosmic Cocktail: Three Parts Dark Matter'' (Science Essentials, 2014, {{ISBN|0691153353}}).<ref name="Siegfried2014">{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/katherine-freese-in-search-of-dark-stars-20140722/|title=In Search of Dark Stars|last=Siegfried|first=Tom|date=2014-07-22|magazine=[[Quanta Magazine]]|access-date=2024-10-27|language=en-US}}</ref> The book is partly autobiographical. She covers the contributions of [[Fritz Zwicky]], for example, who was recently profiled as "the most important astronomer you've never heard of" and "the father of dark matter" on [[Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey]].<ref name="Szokan2014">{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/what-the-universe-is-made-of-probably-narrated-by-a-boa-wearing-physicist/2014/06/02/46e35ef0-e5bb-11e3-a86b-362fd5443d19_story.html|title=What the universe is made of (probably), narrated by a boa-wearing physicist|last=Szokan|first=Nancy|date=2014-06-02|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=2024-10-27|language=en-US}}</ref>

Freese has appeared in seasons 3 and 5 of ''[[Through the Wormhole]]'' with [[Morgan Freeman]].<ref name="Szokan2014" />
